raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|allotropy|151|alloy}}</noinclude>guise: see ''trope''.] The property which certain chemical elements have of existing in two or more distinct forms, each having certain characteristics peculiar to itself. {{smaller|The element carbon, for instance, exists nearly pure in three totally distinct forms—the diamond, graphite, and charcoal.}}

'''allottable''' (a̤-lot′a̤-bl), ''a.''  [< ''allot'' + ''-able''.]  Capable of being allotted.

'''allottee''' (al-o-tē′), ''n.''  [< ''allot'' + ''-ee''<sup>1</sup>.]  One to whom something is allotted, as a plot of ground, shares of stock, or the like.
{{smaller block|The allotment of gardens, which yield a partial support to the ''allottee'', is another means of cheap labor. {{right|''Mayhew.''}}}}

'''allotter''' (a̤-lot′ėr), ''n.'' One who allots or apportions.  ''N. E. D.''

'''allottery†''' (a̤-lot′e-ri), ''n.''  [< ''allot'' + ''-ery'', after ''lottery'', q. v.]  Allotment; what is allotted or assigned to use.
{{smaller block|Give me the poor ''allottery'' my father left me by testament. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 1.}}}}

'''all-over''' (âl-ō′vėr), ''n.''  [See ''all over'', under ''all'', ''adv.'']  The trade-name of a gilt button washed or plated on both the upper and under sides, as distinguished from a ''top'', which is plated or washed on the upper side only.  ''De Colange.''

'''all-overish''' (âl-ō′vėr-ish), ''a.''  [< ''all over'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]  Affecting the whole system; extending all over one: as, an ''all-overish'' feeling of sickness. [Colloq.]

'''all-overishness''' (âl-ō′vėr-ish-nes), ''n.'' A pervasive feeling of uneasiness produced by apprehension or indisposition; general discomfort; malaise. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Our sense of ''all-overishness'' when our friend approaches the edge of a precipice is clearly only a step or two removed from the apprehension or the actual representation of a fall. {{right|''Mind'', IX. 421.}}}}

'''allow<sup>1</sup>''' (a-lou′), ''v.''  [< ME. ''alowen'', ''alouen'', < OF. ''alouer'', ''aloer'', ''aluer'', ''aloier'', assign, allot, place (mod. F. ''allouer'', assign, allow, grant), < ML. ''allocare'', assign, etc.: see ''allocate''. Already in OF. confused in sense and form with another verb, the source of ''allow''<sup>2</sup>, approve, the two being regarded in E. as one word; the separation is merely formal.]  '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To grant, give, or yield; assign; afford: as, to ''allow'' a free passage.
{{smaller block|I am told the gardner is annually ''alowed'' 2000 scudi for the keeping of it. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Nov. 29, 1644.}}}}
{{smaller block|Envy ought, in strict truth, to have no place whatever ''allowed'' it in the heart of man. {{right|''Colton'', Lacon.}}}}
'''2.''' To admit; concede; confess; own; acknowledge: as, to ''allow'' the right of private judgment; he ''allowed'' that he was wrong; he ''allowed'' it might be so.
{{smaller block|<poem>The pow’r of music all our hearts ''allow''.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 382.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The ruin’d spendthrift, now no longer proud,
Claimed kindred there, and had his claims ''allowed''.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil.}}}}
{{smaller block|They’ll not ''allow'' our friend Miss Vermillion to be handsome. {{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|A bright morning so early in the year, she ''allowed'', would generally turn to rain. {{right|''Jane Austen'', Northanger Abbey, p. 61.}}}}
'''3.''' To abate or deduct; take into account; set apart: as, to ''allow'' so much for loss; to ''allow'' a sum for tare or leakage.
{{smaller block|The schedule of tares annexed is the tare to be ''allowed'' in all cases where the invoice tare is not adopted.
{{right|''Circ. of Sec. of U. S. Treasury'', July 14, 1862.}}}}
'''4.''' To grant permission to; permit: as, to ''allow'' a son to be absent.
{{smaller block|No person was ''allowed'' to open a trade or to commence a manufacture . . . unless he had first served his apprenticeship.
{{right|''Froude'', Sketches, p. 170.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Farewell, for longer speech is not ''allow’d.''</poem>
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Balder Dead.}}}}
'''5†.''' To grant special license or indulgence to.
{{smaller block|There is no slander in an ''allowed'' fool.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 5.}}}}
'''6†.''' To invest; intrust.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou shalt be met with thanks,
''Allow’d'' with absolute power.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., v. 2.}}}}
'''7.''' To assert, declare, say; or, of mental assertion, to mean, purpose, intend, or, simply, think: the concessive sense presented assertively. [Colloq., United States.]
{{smaller block|He said he ''allowed'' to work it out.
{{right|''Howells'', Suburban Sketches, p. 58.}}}}
{{smaller block|“I ''’low’d'' maybe dat I might ax yo’ fur ter butt ’gin de tree, and shake ’em down, Sis Cow,” sez Brer Rabbit, sezee.
{{right|''J. C. Harris'', Uncle Remus, p. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|Brer Tarrypin he say wich he wern’t gwine nowhar skasely. Den Brer Rabbit he ''’low'' he wuz on his way to Miss Meadows.
{{right|''J. C. Harris'', Uncle Remus, p. 50.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Allow, Permit, Consent to, Sanction, Suffer, Tolerate.'' ''Allow'' and ''permit'' are often used synonymously; but ''permit'' strictly denotes a formal or implied assent; ''allow'', the absence of an intent, or even only of an attempt, to hinder. ''Consent to'' is formally to permit that which one has the power and generally some disposition to prevent; it implies the assumption of responsibility for that which is thus allowed. ''Sanction'' has a secondary sense of permitting with expressed or implied approbation: as, I cannot ''sanction'' such a course. ''Suffer'' is still more passive or reluctant than ''allow'', and may imply that one does not prevent something, though it is contrary to one’s feelings, judgment, or sense of right. To ''tolerate'' is to bear with something unpleasant: as, I would not ''tolerate'' such impertinence. Many things are ''tolerated'', or ''suffered'', or even ''allowed'', that are not ''permitted'', and many are ''permitted'' that are not really ''consented to'', much less ''sanctioned''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And when the Queen petition’d for his leave
To see the hunt, ''allow’d'' it easily.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For crimes are but ''permitted'', not decreed.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Cym. and Iph., l. 475.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Scourge the bad revolting stars,
That have ''consented unto'' Henry’s death!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Constantine certainly ''sanctioned'' what are called pious uses. {{right|''H. Binney'', Vidal versus City of Phila.}}}}
{{smaller block|Jesus answering said unto him, ''Suffer'' it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness.
{{right|Mat. iii. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|They cannot understand the complex feeling that finds relief in sarcasm and allegory, that ''tolerates'' the frivolous and the vain as an ironic reading of the lesson of life.
{{right|''Shorthouse'', Little Schoolmaster Mark, p. 49.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To make abatement, concession, or provision: followed by ''for'': as, to ''allow for'' the tare.
{{smaller block|''Allowing'' still ''for'' the different ways of making it.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
'''2.''' To permit; admit: with ''of'': as, “''of'' this ''allow'',” ''Shak.'', W. T., iv. (cho.).

{{smaller block|Thou shalt hold the opinion of Pythagoras, ere I will ''allow of'' thy wits.{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Court, which is the best and surest judge of writing, has generally ''allowed of'' verse; and in the town it has found favourers of wit and quality.{{right|''Dryden'', Ded. of Ess. on Dram. Poesy.}}}}

'''allow<sup>2</sup>†''' (a-lou′), ''v. t.''  [< ME. ''alouen'', ''alowen'', < OF. ''alouer'', praise, later ''allouer'', < L. ''allaudare'', ''adlaudare'', praise, < ''ad'', to, + ''laudare'', praise: see ''laud'', ''v.''; cf. OF. ''loer'', ''louer'', approve, < L. ''laudare''. Early confused in sense and form with ''allow''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. Doublet, ''allaud''.]  To praise or commend; approve, justify, or sanction.
{{smaller block|Ye ''allow'' the deeds of your fathers.{{right|Luke xi. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|That same framing of his stile, to an old rustick language, I dare not ''alowe''.{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie.}}}}
{{smaller block|If your grace ''allow'' me for a preacher, I would desire your grace to give me leave to discharge my conscience.{{right|''Latimer'', 3d Serm. bef. Edw. VI.}}}}

'''allowable<sup>1</sup>''' (a-lou′a-bl), ''a.''  [< ''allow''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able'', after F. ''allouable'', < ML. ''allocabilis'', < ''allocare'': see ''allocate''.]  Proper to be or capable of being allowed or permitted; not forbidden; legitimate; permissible: as, a certain degree of freedom is ''allowable'' among friends.
{{smaller block|In actions of this sort, the light of nature alone may discover that which is in the sight of God ''allowable''.{{right|''Hooker''.}}}}

'''allowable<sup>2</sup>†''' (a-lou′a-bl), ''a.''  [< ME. ''allowable'', ''alowable'', < ''alowen'', praise: see ''allow''<sup>2</sup> and ''-able''. Mixed with ''allowable''<sup>1</sup>.]  Praiseworthy; laudable; worthy of sanction or approval; satisfactory; acceptable. {{smaller block|Custom had made it not only excusable but ''allowable.''
{{right|''Bp. Sanderson'', Sermons, Ad. Mag., ii. § 8. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''allowableness''' (a̤-lou′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being allowable; exemption from prohibition; freedom from impropriety; lawfulness.
{{smaller block|I cannot think myself engaged . . . to discourse of lots, as to their nature, use, and ''allowableness;'' and that not only in matters of moment and business, but also of recreation.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, I. viii.}}}}

'''allowably''' (a̤-lou′a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an allowable manner; with propriety.

'''allowance<sup>1</sup>''' (a̤-lou′a̤ns), ''n.''  [< ME. ''alouance, alowans'', < OF. ''alouance'', < ''alouer'': see ''allow''<sup>1</sup> and ''-ance''.]  '''1.''' Sanction; approval; tolerance: as, the ''allowance'' of slavery.
{{smaller block|See what ''allowance'' vice finds in the respectable and well-conditioned class.
{{right|''Emerson'', Conduct of Life.}}}}
'''2.''' Admission or acceptance; a conceding or granting: as, the ''allowance'' of a claim.
{{smaller block|Or what if I were to allow — would it not be a singular ''allowance?'' — that our furniture should be more complex than the Arab’s in proportion as we are morally and intellectually his superior?
{{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 40.}}}}
'''3.''' Allotment; apportionment; a definite sum or quantity set apart or granted, such as alimony: as, an ''allowance'' by a husband to a wife; an ''allowance'' of grog or tobacco to a seaman; an ''allowance'' of pocket-money.
{{smaller block|And his [Jehoiachin’s] ''allowance'' was a continual ''allowance'' given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life.
{{right|2 Ki. xxv. 30.}}}}
'''4.''' Specifically, in ''law'', an extra sum awarded besides regular costs to the successful party in a difficult case.—'''5.''' A deduction: as, the ''allowances'' made in commerce for tare, breakages, etc.—'''6.''' An abatement or addition on account of some extenuating, qualifying, enhancing, or other circumstance: as, to make ''allowances'' for a person’s youth or inexperience; ''allowance'' for difference of time; ''allowance'' for shrinkage of values, etc.
{{smaller block|But even these monstrosities are interesting and instructive; nay, many of them, if we can but make ''allowance'' for different ways of thought and language, contain germs of truth and rays of light.
{{right|''Max Müller'', India, p. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|The saints and demi-gods whom history worships we are constrained to accept with a grain of ''allowance''.
{{right|''Emerson'', Essays, 1st ser., p. 268.}}}}

'''7.''' In ''minting'', a permissible deviation in the fineness and weight of coins, owing to the difficulty of securing exact conformity to the standard prescribed by law. {{smaller|In the United States the allowance for the fineness of gold coins is .001, and for weight a quarter of a grain to each one-dollar piece; in silver coins the allowance for fineness is .003, and for weight 1½ grains to each coin. In the gold coinage of France the allowance for both fineness and weight is .002, and of England .002 for fineness and two grains in each sovereign for weight. Also called ''remedy'' and ''tolerance'' (which see).}}—'''Barrack allowance.''' {{smaller|See ''barrack''.}}—'''Compassionate allowance.''' {{smaller|See ''compassionate''.}}

'''allowance<sup>1</sup>''' (a-lou′ans), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''allowanced'', ppr. ''allowancing''.  [< ''allowance''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']  To put upon allowance; limit to a certain fixed periodic amount of anything: as, to ''allowance'' a spendthrift; distress compelled the captain of the ship to ''allowance'' his crew.
{{smaller block|You have had as much as you can eat, you’re asked if you want any more, and you answer “No.” Then don’t you ever go and say you were ''allowanced'', mind that.
{{right|''Dickens'', Old Curiosity Shop, xxxvi.}}}}

'''allowance<sup>2</sup>''' (a̤-lou′ans), ''n.''  [< ME. ''allowaunce'', < OF. ''alouance'', < ''alouer'': see ''allow''<sup>2</sup> and ''-ance''. Mixed with ''allowance''<sup>1</sup>.]  '''1†.''' Praise; commendation.
{{smaller block|It is not the ''allowance'' or applause of men that I seek.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Hard Texts, p. 259.}}}}
'''2.''' Sanction; approbation; authorization: as, a judge’s ''allowance'' of a compromise or settlement of a case by the parties interested.
{{smaller block|<poem>You sent a large commission
To Gregory de Cassalis to conclude,
Without the king’s will, or the state’s ''allowance'',
A league between his highness and Ferrara.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iii. 2.}}}}
'''3†.''' Reputation.
{{smaller block|<poem>His bark is stoutly timber’d, and his pilot
Of very expert and approv’d ''allowance''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 1.}}}}

'''allowedly''' (a̤-lou′ed-li), ''adv.'' Admittedly.
{{smaller block|Lord Lyttleton is ''allowedly'' the author of these dialogues.
{{right|''Shenstone'', Works, III. cii.}}}}

'''allower''' (a̤-lou′ėr), ''n.'' One who allows, permits, grants, or authorizes.

'''alloxan''' (a-lok′sa̤n), ''n.''  [< ''all''(''antoin'') + ''ox''(''alic'') + ''-an'': so named because it contains the elements of allantoin and oxalic acid.]  One of the products (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) of the decomposition of uric acid by nitric acid. {{smaller|When treated with alkalis it produces alloxanic acid. In contact with ammonia it produces purpurate of ammonia, identical with murexid, which with various mordants produces reds and purples on silk and wool. This was much used in 1855 and 1856, but was soon superseded by aniline colors.}}

'''alloxanate''' (a-lok′sạ-nāt), ''n.''  [< ''alloxanic'' + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.]  A salt formed by the union of alloxanic acid and a base.

'''alloxanic''' (al-ok-san′ik), ''a.''  [< ''alloxan'' + ''-ic.'']  Pertaining to or produced from alloxan: as, ''alloxanic'' acid.—{{smaller|'''Alloxanic acid,''' a strong crystalline dibasic acid produced by the action of alkalis on alloxan. On boiling, its salts decompose into urea and mesoxalates.}}

'''alloxantin''' (al-ok-san′tin), ''n.''  [< ''alloxan(t-)'' + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]  A white crystalline substance (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>4</sub>O<sub>7</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O) obtained when alloxan is brought into contact with reducing agents. Oxidizing agents reconvert it into alloxan. Also called ''uroxin.''

'''alloy''' (a-loi′), ''v.''  [< F. ''aloyer'', earlier ''allayer'', < OF. ''aleier'', ''alier'', < L. ''alligare'', combine: see ''allay''<sup>2</sup> (of which ''alloy'' is the recent form, based on mod. F.) and ''ally''<sup>1</sup>. The sense has been influenced by the erroneous etymology from F. ''à loi:'' see ''alloy'', ''n.'']  '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To mix (two or more metals) so as to form a compound, without reference to the relative value of the metals mixed.
{{smaller block|When we wish to ''alloy'' three or more metals, we often experience difficulties, either because one of the metals is more oxidisable, or denser, or more fusible than the others, or because there is no direct affinity between two of the metals.
{{right|''Ure'', Dict., I. 92.}}}}
'''2.''' To reduce to a desired standard or quality by mixing with a less valuable metal: as, to ''alloy'' gold or silver with copper.—'''3.''' Figuratively, to debase or reduce in character or condition by<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
